title: Harvey Mason, Rufus Reid & More Are Named 2027 NEA Jazz Masters: Full List
summary: They'll be honored at a tribute concert in Washington, D.C., in April.
contentText:
Harvey Mason has watched his son Harvey Mason Jr. become CEO of the Recording Academy and one of the most visible people in the music field. But jazz fans know Mason Sr. as a celebrated drummer, composer and producer in this own right. And now he’s a Jazz Master, so declared by The National Endowment for the Arts.

The Jazz Masters Fellowship is the nation’s highest honor in jazz. The Arts Endowment, in collaboration with the DC Jazz Festival, will honor this year’s five recipients in a tribute concert on Monday, April 5, at Arena Stage in Washington, D.C., and streamed online.

Here’s a look at this year’s five honorees:

- Terry Gibbs , 102, is a vibraphonist, bandleader and composer. Over the course of his long career, he recorded more than 80 albums, composed more than 300 works and led the Dream Band.

- John Edward Hasse , 78, is a scholar, writer and pianist. Hasse is the recipient of the 2027 A.B. Spellman NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship for Jazz Advocacy. He is also a two-time Grammy nominee, for best historical album and best album notes, both in 1989 for The Classic Hoagy Carmichael . Hasse is the founder of the Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra and Jazz Appreciation Month.

- Harvey Mason , 79, is a drummer, composer and producer. Mason is a 10-time Grammy nominee, counting both solo work and his role in the group Fourplay. He received at least one nomination in four consecutive decades beginning in the 1970s. His nominations span pop, R&B, jazz and contemporary jazz categories. Mason has contributed to more than 1,300 recordings.

- Rufus Reid , 82, is a bassist, composer and educator. He is a two-time Grammy nominee, both in 2015, for best large jazz ensemble album for Quiet Pride: The Elizabeth Catlett Project and best instrumental composition for “Recognition.” Reid has made significant contributions to jazz as both a performing artist and a teacher. He helped establish a pioneering university jazz studies program at William Paterson University in Wayne, N.J.

- Dr. Larry Ridley , 89, is a jazz bassist and educator. His career has included leading jazz education and advocacy initiatives, including the development of Rutgers University’s jazz performance programs, founding the Jazz Legacy Ensemble and an annual concert series at the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture in New York City’s Harlem.

“Through their remarkable artistry, leadership and dedication to nurturing future generations, the 2027 National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Masters have worked to advance the distinctly American art form of jazz,” Mary Anne Carter, chairman of the Arts Endowment, said in a statement. “We look forward to partnering with the DC Jazz Festival to celebrate their contributions and the enduring power of jazz.”

“The DC Jazz Festival is deeply honored to partner with the National Endowment for the Arts in celebrating these five extraordinary Jazz Masters,” said Sunny Sumter, president and CEO of the DC Jazz Festival. “Through artistry, innovation and lifelong dedication, these remarkable individuals have influenced generations, preserving jazz’s rich legacy while inspiring its future.”

Since 1982, the National Endowment for the Arts has awarded 186 fellowships to leading figures in jazz. The fellowships, awarded only to living individuals, are $25,000 and can be received just once in a lifetime.
